status: cited: built from published surveys, papers and case studies; verified 38/40 figures against their sources
unit: engineer-minutes, one experienced engineer, hands-on time only (no waiting, fabrication or meetings)

per_change.derivation:
Example change: a heavier payload forces a larger joint-2 servo. That touches links and brackets, the simulations, the power budget and possibly the PCB, plus the BOM, drawings and manual pages.
- Low 8 h: about one fingertip redesign-and-verify cycle (6-8 h, Wolniakowski et al.).
- Typical 24 h: 3 working days, the low end of Honarpardaz's 3-4 working days per manual finger-design iteration.
- High 80 h: 10 working days. Terwiesch & Loch found the hands-on activity in one engineering change order 'does not exceed 10 days'. This also matches roughly one PCB re-spin when the change reaches the board (Lifecycle Insights via Mentor: 2.9 re-spins per project at about 5.5-8.5 days each; the two versions conflict).

Elapsed-time figures are deliberately excluded: Terwiesch & Loch's 2 months to over a year per change, and Langer et al.'s self-reported mean of 60.6 working days (SD 140).

Scale context: engineering changes take about 31% of R&D capacity (Langer et al., n=27), and Soderberg (via Terwiesch & Loch) reported about 45% of engineering time going to changing parts that were 'thought to be ready'.

steps.label: Requirements + spec
steps.long_label: Requirements and spec (payload, reach, DOF, joint-torque sizing, architecture choice)
steps.derivation: Estimate, informed by the 2019 Embedded Markets Study. No source gives hours for writing a spec for a small robot arm. Low is 4 h: a one-page requirements list with no review. Typical is 12 h (1.5 days): requirements, reach and payload numbers, joint-torque sizing to pick actuators, and a controller/architecture choice. High is 64 h. In the 2019 bars of the 'What percentage of your design time is spent on each stage?' chart (p.38, N=424), 'Developing system specs' is 13% against 31% for 'Detailed design'. I read the 13% myself from the same chart that holds the verified 31% and 19% figures; the 2019 values add to 99%. Applying that 13/31 ratio to this baseline's typical detailed-design effort (CAD 56 h + electronics 57 h + firmware 40 h = 153 h) gives about 64 h. Typical is set well below that ratio because a small team writes lighter specs than the ~16-engineer, ~12-month projects in that survey. Context: a 2006 Flomerics survey named design requirement changes (59%) as the top cause of PCB schedule overruns.

steps.label: Mechanical CAD (arm + gripper)
steps.long_label: Mechanical CAD: 5-DOF arm plus force-sensing gripper (one revision)
steps.derivation:
GRIPPER (low 8 h / typical 16 h / high 80 h):
- Low 8 h: Kuhn-Stoff's average design time for one custom AM gripper hand, a vendor CEO estimate for adapting finger geometry on an existing base gripper.
- Typical 16 h: two fingertips at the 6-8 h per fingertip an expert engineer reported in Wolniakowski et al. (2020), which includes 3D-print verification. Taken as 2 x 8 h, with sensor mounting absorbed into that figure.
- High 80 h: about 2 weeks (10 workdays x 8 h), Honarpardaz's figure for manually designing one industrial finger at 3-4 working days per iteration. The same researcher told LiU it takes 'at least a month' for an expert, so 80 h is the conservative end.

ARM (low 24 h / typical 40 h / high 120 h): estimate only. No verified source gives hours for CAD of a whole 5-DOF arm. Assumes about 12-20 custom parts (base, turntable, shoulder/elbow/wrist links, servo brackets, covers).
- Low: 12 parts x 2 h.
- Typical: 16 parts x 2.5 h.
- High: 20 parts x 6 h, using the 6-8 h-per-fingertip figure as the per-part ceiling for complex parts.

Totals:
- Low: 8 + 24 = 32 h.
- Typical: 16 + 40 = 56 h (about 7 workdays).
- High: 80 + 120 = 200 h.

This covers one revision only. Rework from changes is in per_change_iteration.

steps.label: Simulation setup + runs
steps.long_label: Simulation: build MJCF/URDF from CAD, then pick-and-place, payload, workspace and shake runs
steps.derivation:
Estimate. Published sources describe robot-model setup as manual and hard but give no hours for it. In Tola & Corke's 2023 survey, 67% of URDF users wrote URDFs by hand and 89% rated creating them medium or difficult. In Afzal et al. (2020), 34% of developers skipped simulation on a project, and 53.6% of those cited lack of time or resources.

Components:
- Model build (export meshes, inertias, joint limits, actuators, contacts): low 4 h, typical 8 h, high 24 h.
- Four test scenarios, each scripted, run and post-processed: low 2 h each, typical 4 h each, high 8 h each, so 8 / 16 / 32 h.

Totals: low 12 h, typical 24 h, high 56 h.

Compute time is not counted. In Sandia's analysis, running the simulation was 4% of analyst engineering time, with about 91% going to setup steps. Tech-Clarity found preprocessing takes 38% of simulation time, against 23% waiting for the solver.

Cross-check: the Embedded Markets Study puts the simulation stage at 6% of design time against 31% for detailed design. Applied to this baseline's 153 h of detailed design, that gives about 30 h, so the 24 h typical is conservative.

Not used as a baseline: DAA's 63 h of preprocessing for one FEA iteration, and Sandia's 317-1,798 h per analysis. Both are heavy FEA work, not MuJoCo rigid-body simulation.

steps.derivation:
Anchored on PCB layout hours that the original designers reported for real boards (Bazeghi et al. 2007, layout only).
- Three 2-layer boards took 12, 32 and 40 h.
- A 90-component motor driver took 21 h.
- The largest small board took 68 h.
- A 5-DOF arm controller (MCU, servo bus/motor drivers, regulators, load-cell amplifier, connectors; roughly 60-120 parts) is comparable to boards B11, B4, B8 and B9.

Layout: low 12 h (the smallest 2-layer board), typical 32 h (the median 2-layer board), high 68 h (the largest small board).

Schematic and part selection, scaled from Feranec's logged hours (95 h schematic, 50 h component research, 215 h layout):
- Schematic = 0.44 x layout. This is conservative: excluding the DDR3 routing, the ratio would be about 0.8.
- Component research = 0.23 x layout.
- Harness design is an estimate: 2 / 4 / 8 h.

Totals:
- Low: 12 + 5 + 3 + 2 = 22 h.
- Typical: 32 + 14 + 7 + 4 = 57 h.
- High: 68 + 30 + 16 + 8 = 122 h.

Calendar context, not counted here: Predictable Designs gives 2-5 weeks each for schematic and layout plus 1-4 weeks for critical part selection. The Aberdeen survey for Siemens averages about 3 months from schematic to manufacturing release. Fabrication alone is at least 24 h at JLCPCB, plus shipping.

steps.label: Firmware
steps.long_label: Firmware: servo bus driver, joint control/IK, gripper force loop, host comms, bring-up
steps.derivation:
Estimate, informed by two sources. Predictable Designs puts firmware/software at 1-6 months of calendar time for a commercial hardware product. The 2019 Embedded Markets Study splits design time into 19% testing and debugging versus 31% detailed design, so debugging is about 0.6x the design effort.
- Typical 40 h: about 25 h writing code plus about 15 h test and debug (0.61 x 25).
- Low 16 h: reuse the vendor servo library; about 10 h writing plus 6 h debug.
- High 160 h: the low end of Predictable Designs' range, treating 1 calendar month as about 4 x 40 h of full-time effort.

The Embedded study's 12.2-month average project (teams of about 16 engineers) is not used, because it would overstate the scope.

steps.label: BOM + sourcing
steps.long_label: BOM with vendor sourcing: find parts and supplier models, price, check availability, alternates
steps.derivation:
Assumes a BOM of about 60-150 lines: servos, bearings, fasteners, shafts and electronics. Electronic component research is already counted under electronics.

Pricing, anchored on the CalcuQuote/Phase Electronics case (about 2 h to price a 100-line BOM by hand; a variant says 2-3 h):
- Low: 60 lines, 1.2 h.
- Typical: 100 lines, 2 h.
- High: 150 lines at 3 h per 100, 4.5 h.

Searching for standard and supplier parts and their CAD models: 2 / 5 / 12 h. In CADENAS's 2022 survey, 52% reported 30 min/day and 48% reported 1 h/day or more, which implies a mean of about 0.9 h/day. Only part of that is counted here, to avoid double-counting with CAD.

Compiling the BOM, alternates and vendor carts: 1 / 3 / 7.5 h.

Totals: about 4 / 10 / 24 h.

Context, not added: in Fictiv x MISUMI 2026, 83% of 321 director-level respondents said their typical engineer spends 4+ hours a week on sourcing, quoting and ordering. In Accuris 2026, 77% of 439 respondents said they spend 5+ hours a week reading datasheets and comparing alternatives. In Tech-Clarity 2021, searching for information such as specs, BOMs and supplier data was 23% of non-value-added time, or about 7.6% of all engineering time.

Waiting is NOT counted. A conventional manufacturer takes 2-3 days to return a quote (Polyverse testimonial on Protolabs), and Xometry's S-1 says 'days or weeks' to finalize price and lead time. headlines.text: An expert engineer estimated that designing just one robot-gripper fingertip by hand takes 6-8 hours, including 3D-print checks (Wolniakowski et al., ROBOVIS 2020).

In Sandia's analysis of design-through-analysis work, running the simulation took only 4% of analysts' engineering time; about 91% went to setup such as CAD cleanup, geometry decomposition and meshing (Sandia National Laboratories, SAND2005-4647, 2005).
Laying out even a small 2-layer circuit board took 12-40 engineer-hours, before any schematic or part selection (Bazeghi et al., IFIP/IEEE VLSI-SoC 2007).
83% of manufacturing leaders say their typical engineer spends 4+ hours every week on supplier sourcing, quoting and ordering (Fictiv x MISUMI State of Manufacturing Report, 2026).
Handling engineering changes uses up about 31% of manufacturers' R&D capacity (Langer et al., DESIGN 2012 survey of Danish companies).

caveats:
TOTALS. One design revision by one experienced engineer at 8 h/day, excluding per-change work:
- Low: 6,570 min, about 110 h (about 14 workdays).
- Typical: 14,460 min, about 241 h (about 30 workdays, or 6 work-weeks).
- High: 44,740 min, about 746 h (about 4.5 months).
Each later design change adds about 1,440 min (3 days) typical, with a range of 480-4,800 min.

WHAT IS COUNTED. These are hands-on engineer-minutes only. The baseline leaves out:
- Waiting and calendar time: RFQ turnaround of 2-3 days to weeks, PCB fabrication of at least 24 h plus shipping, Aberdeen's 5.4 days to build a prototype, and change orders that take months elapsed.
- Physical printing, machining and assembly.
- Review meetings.
On calendar time the gap would look much larger. Predictable Designs gives 2-5 weeks each for schematic and layout and 1-6 months for firmware, and the Aberdeen survey for Siemens averages about 3 months from schematic to release. Do not put a calendar figure next to Morph's ~1 minute without labelling it.

WHERE THE DATA IS THIN. Several numbers are my estimates, informed by the cited sources rather than taken from them:
- Arm CAD: only gripper and finger figures exist.
- MuJoCo/MJCF setup: surveys show it is manual and hard but give no hours.
- Firmware, spec, harness, print slicing, and RFQ prep effort.
The 13% "developing system specs" share is not one of the pre-verified figures. I read it myself from the same p.38 chart of the verified 2019 Embedded Markets Study; the 2019 bars add to 99%.

VENDOR SOURCES. Many figures come from vendor-run or vendor-sponsored surveys and case studies: Fictiv, Accuris, CADENAS, Tech-Clarity, CalcuQuote, trinckle, Protolabs and Mentor/Lifecycle Insights. Cite them as such. The two conflicting Lifecycle Insights versions (8.5 days vs about 5.5 days per re-spin) are why only ranges are used.

FIGURES NOT TO STRETCH. Do not apply these directly to this robot:
- Sandia's 317-1,798 h per analysis.
- DAA's 63 h of FEA preprocessing.
- NIST's 60.3 h cycle, which is mostly the supplier re-modelling parts from drawings.
- The Embedded study's 12.2-month projects.
- Langer's 60.6 working days.
Rejected figures, not used: Robinson 2010 / IEEE "39 days", and roboticscenter.ai's SO-101 times.

FRAMING FOR THE PITCH. Morph's output is a first draft that an engineer still has to review. For an honest before/after card, add review time to the "after" side, for example "~1 min to generate + a few hours of engineer review vs ~6 work-weeks (typical) by hand". No verified IDC or McKinsey "time spent searching" figure was found, so don't use the commonly repeated IDC search-time statistic.

verified_figures.source: Modern practices in PCB design verification (citing Lifecycle Insights, Sept 2018)

verified_figures.step: electronics_pcb: PCB layout effort for small boards (measured)
verified_figures.claim: A peer-reviewed study recorded actual layout effort for 12 commercial PCBs. The 11 small boards took 12 to 68 engineering hours each, for layout alone. The three 2-layer boards took 12, 32 and 40 hours. A motor driver board took 21 hours and a motor controller board took 43 hours.
verified_figures.value: 12-68 hours layout-only for small boards (2-layer boards: 12, 32, 40 h; motor driver 21 h; motor controller 43 h); 400 h for an 8-layer network appliance
verified_figures.unit: engineering-hours (PCB layout only, excluding schematic)
verified_figures.source: Estimating Design Time for System Circuits (Bazeghi et al.)

verified_figures.step: electronics_pcb: schematic + layout + prototype + firmware calendar time (small-team product)
verified_figures.claim: A hardware product-development consultant gives these typical calendar times for a new electronic product: schematic 2-5 weeks, PCB layout 2-5 weeks, ordering prototypes 1-2 weeks, evaluating and debugging prototypes 5+ weeks, firmware 1-6 months.
verified_figures.value: Schematic 2-5 wk; PCB layout 2-5 wk; prototype order 1-2 wk; prototype evaluation/debug 5+ wk; firmware 1-6 months
verified_figures.unit: calendar weeks / months
verified_figures.source: Product Development Timeline: How Long It Takes to Develop a New Hardware Product

verified_figures.step: electronics_pcb: PCB design cycle time (industry survey)
verified_figures.claim: In a PCB design survey, half of respondents said a new PCB design takes 6-12 weeks from concept to final testing and manufacturing signoff. 29% said more than 12 weeks and 21% said less than 6 weeks.
verified_figures.value: 6-12 weeks (50% of respondents); >12 weeks (29%); <6 weeks (21%)
verified_figures.unit: weeks per new PCB design (concept to manufacturing signoff)
verified_figures.source: Flomerics Releases PCB Design Survey Results

verified_figures.step: electronics_pcb: schematic-to-manufacturing-release time (recent survey)
verified_figures.claim: A 2023 Aberdeen Research survey commissioned by Siemens found that designs take about 3 months on average from completed schematic to manufacturing release, regardless of company size or industry.
verified_figures.unit: months per design (schematic to PCB assembly / manufacturing release)
verified_figures.source: Are you normal? (summarizing Aberdeen 'PCB Design Best Practices in 2023')

verified_figures.step: electronics_pcb: embedded project duration and firmware test/debug share (bring-up proxy)
verified_figures.claim: In a large survey of embedded engineers, the last completed embedded project took 12.2 months on average. Testing and debugging took 19% of design time and detailed design took 31%. 61% of projects finished late or were cancelled. Average team size was 16.1 engineers.
verified_figures.value: 12.2 months average project; 19% of design time on testing & debugging (~2.3 months, derived); 61% late or cancelled
verified_figures.unit: months; % of design time; % of projects
verified_figures.source: 2019 Embedded Markets Study (EETimes / Embedded.com)

verified_figures.step: electronics_pcb: schematic and layout hours logged on a real board (upper bound)
verified_figures.claim: An experienced hardware designer logged his hours on one board: 95 hours of schematic design (72 h drawing + 23 h checking), 215 hours of PCB layout, and about 50 hours of component research (parts, availability, footprints).
verified_figures.value: 95 h schematic; 215 h PCB layout; ~50 h component research (~360 h total)
verified_figures.unit: engineering-hours
verified_figures.source: Do you know how long schematic design and PCB layout take?

verified_figures.step: electronics_pcb: physical respin turnaround floor (fab time per iteration)
verified_figures.claim: Even the fastest low-cost board house needs about 24 hours to make 5 small 2-layer prototype boards, and 1-2 days for under 50 pieces. Shipping, assembly and re-test come on top, so each physical respin adds days to weeks.
verified_figures.value: 24 hours (5 pcs, 1-2 layer, <=100x100 mm); 1-2 days (<50 pcs); 5-6 days (>=50 pcs)
verified_figures.unit: production time (excludes shipping and assembly)
verified_figures.source: PCB Fabrication Services and Production Time (JLCPCB Help Center)

verified_figures.step: sourcing_bom: supplier sourcing, quoting and supplier management
verified_figures.claim: 83% of engineers spend 4 or more hours every week on supplier sourcing, quoting and quality management. In the same survey, 93% say engineering productivity would improve if they could offload sourcing.
verified_figures.unit: hours per engineer per week (reported by 83% of respondents)
verified_figures.source: 2026 State of Manufacturing & Supply Chain Report ('Your Engineers Are Spending 4+ Hours a Week on Procurement')

verified_figures.step: sourcing_bom: component selection / datasheet research
verified_figures.claim: 77% of engineering professionals spend five or more hours per week reading datasheets and comparing component alternatives.
verified_figures.unit: hours per week (reported by 77% of respondents)
verified_figures.source: The Hidden Tax on Engineering Teams: What Inaction on Parts Intelligence Actually Costs (citing an independent survey by Fuld & Company, March 2026)

verified_figures.step: sourcing_bom: searching for standard / supplier parts
verified_figures.claim: 48% of engineers spend at least one hour per day searching for standard or supplier parts. The answers were: 30 min 52.3%, 1 hour 31.9%, 2 hours 12%, 3 hours 3.8%. The report models search as 27% of engineering time, and search, configuring and recreating parts together as 68%, or 1,251 hours per year per engineer.
verified_figures.unit: hour or more per day searching for parts (48% of engineers); search = 27% of time
verified_figures.source: 2022 Engineering Efficiency Report: 6 Opportunities to Kick your Engineering into High Gear

verified_figures.step: sourcing_bom: searching for / recreating supplier part models
verified_figures.claim: Engineers each lose 1.82 hours a day searching for or recreating supplier parts in their design systems. That is 59 working days per engineer per year, or almost 20% of engineering time.
verified_figures.unit: hours per engineer per day (about 59 working days per year)
verified_figures.source: 2015 Engineering Design Efficiency Report Reveals Engineers Waste 59 Days Per Year (press release)

verified_figures.step: sourcing_bom: non-value-added engineering time (searching for information, BOMs, supplier info)
verified_figures.claim: Engineers waste a third of their time on non-value-added work and spend only 54% on design. The largest share of that waste, 23%, is searching for information, which the report says includes BOMs, supplier information and components. Another 15% is recreating data that couldn't be found.
verified_figures.unit: % of non-value-added time spent searching for information (non-value-added work = 33% of total time, so about 7.6% of all engineering time)
verified_figures.source: How-To Reduce Non-Value-Added Work in Engineering (eBook)

verified_figures.step: sourcing_bom: BOM creation and cost estimating share of engineering week
verified_figures.claim: At build-to-order and engineer-to-order manufacturers, creating bills of material takes 14% of engineers' week. Creating cost estimates takes 4% and pricing orders another 4%.
verified_figures.unit: % of engineers' weekly time creating BOMs (plus 4% cost estimates and 4% pricing)
verified_figures.source: Report: Engineers Spend More Than Half of Time on Low-Value Activity (summarizing Cincom 'Best Practices: Mass Customization and Build-to-Order Manufacturing')

verified_figures.step: sourcing_bom: manually pricing / costing an electronics BOM
verified_figures.claim: An EMS company pricing quotes by hand in spreadsheets needed about 2 hours to price out a 100-line BOM. With quoting software it took 10–15 minutes.
verified_figures.unit: hours to manually price a 100-line BOM (vs 10–15 min automated)
verified_figures.source: Phase Electronics customer story (formerly CalcuQuote case study)

verified_figures.step: Manufacturing quotes (traditional RFQ vs instant quote)
verified_figures.claim: In traditional custom-parts sourcing, finalizing price and lead time through RFQs takes days to weeks. Xometry's instant quoting engine prices CAD uploads in real time and analyzes geometry in seconds.
verified_figures.value: days to weeks (traditional) vs seconds (instant)
verified_figures.unit: elapsed time per order to get a firm price and lead time
verified_figures.source: Xometry, Inc. Form S-1 Registration Statement (Business section)

verified_figures.step: Manufacturing quotes (traditional RFQ vs instant quote)
verified_figures.claim: A customer case study says conventional manufacturers take 2-3 days to return a quote and lead time. On Protolabs, uploading the model gives price and lead time immediately.
verified_figures.unit: days per quote (conventional manufacturer), vs immediate/seconds (instant)
verified_figures.source: Polyverse Solutions case study: Multi-Process Manufacturing Helps Bring New Machinery to Market Faster

verified_figures.step: Supplier sourcing/quoting overhead (engineer time)
verified_figures.claim: 83% of engineers spend 4 or more hours every week on supplier sourcing, quoting and quality management. 81% of manufacturing leaders call supplier sourcing and management too time-consuming.
verified_figures.value: 4+ (reported by 83% of engineers)
verified_figures.unit: hours per week
verified_figures.source: 2026 State of Manufacturing & Supply Chain Report

verified_figures.step: Manufacturing documentation: 2D drawings / design annotation
verified_figures.claim: In a NIST controlled study, annotating a fully dimensioned 2D engineering drawing took 2.2-3.1 hours per machined part (53-84 characteristics each). Across design annotation, manufacture and inspection, the drawing-based cycle averaged 60.3 hours per part, versus 15.2 hours for the model-based cycle (a 74.8% reduction).
verified_figures.value: 2.2-3.1 hrs drawing annotation per part; 60.3 hrs total drawing-based cycle vs 15.2 hrs model-based
verified_figures.unit: hours per part
verified_figures.source: Hedberg T., Lubell J., Fischer L., Maggiano L., Barnard Feeney A., 'Testing the Digital Thread in Support of Model-Based Manufacturing and Inspection', J. Computing and Information Science in Engineering 16(2):021001

verified_figures.step: Manufacturing documentation: CAM programming
verified_figures.claim: A professional CAM programmer took 30 minutes (simple part, 4 machined features) to 57-60 minutes (multi-axis part, 19 features) to program a one-off aluminium part from a 3D model. Working from 2D drawings only, it took 130-152 minutes. Tool preparation added another 150 minutes per part.
verified_figures.value: 30-60 min (from 3D model); 130-152 min (from 2D drawing); +150 min tool prep
verified_figures.unit: minutes per part
verified_figures.source: Uski P., Ellman A., Laine I., Hillman L., Nieminen J., 'Model-Based Definition Accelerates Product Life Cycle in Manufacturing and Inspection Phase - Experiment of Machined One-Off Production', Proceedings of the Design Society (DESIGN 2022)

verified_figures.step: Assembly instructions / work instructions authoring
verified_figures.claim: An industry estimating guide budgets 3-5 hours per page to write an operator's or procedure manual for a new product or system (interviews, writing, photos/graphics, editing, index). It adds about 10 hours to design a template if none exists.
verified_figures.value: 3-5 (plus ~10 hrs one-time template)
verified_figures.unit: hours per page
verified_figures.source: A Guide to Estimating Writing Projects (V4.0)

verified_figures.step: Physical assembly of an open-source robot arm (SO-100)
verified_figures.claim: Hugging Face's official LeRobot SO-100 guide says the first arm takes a bit more than 1 hour to assemble and later arms under 1 hour. Motor ID/baudrate setup and calibration are separate steps on top of that.
verified_figures.value: ~1+ (first arm); <1 (subsequent arm)
verified_figures.unit: hours per arm (mechanical assembly only)
verified_figures.source: LeRobot documentation: SO-100
